html:
The Great Famine of Mount Lebanon was a mass starvation in the mountains of Lebanon during the First World War, from 1915 to 1918. Estimates of the dead run up to about half of Mount Lebanon's people, around 200,000, though the true toll is uncertain.

Mount Lebanon was a self-governing district of the Ottoman Empire. Its people, mostly Maronite Christians and Druze, grew silk and imported much of their grain. The war cut that supply.

  • The Allied fleet blockaded the coast.
  • The Ottoman commander Djemal Pasha took control of the region and requisitioned grain and animals for the army, and blocked food from Syria's interior.
  • A locust plague in 1915 stripped the crops.
  • Hoarding, high prices and typhus did the rest.

Many Lebanese remember the famine as a deliberate Ottoman policy; historians still argue how far it was. It drove a new wave of emigration to the Americas and fed support for the French Mandate that followed.
